title: Insert Interval — Single-Pass Insertion into a Sorted List
summary: Inserting a single new range into an already-merged, sorted interval list without re-sorting or re-merging from scratch — the incremental counterpart to Merge Intervals.

slides.markdown:
You have a calendar that's already merged and sorted — no overlaps, no gaps to clean up — and one new event arrives. Do you really need to re-sort and re-merge the whole thing?

No. **Insert Interval** exploits the fact that the existing list is already sorted: a single O(n) pass splits it into three zones — intervals entirely before the new one, intervals that overlap it, and intervals entirely after — and rebuilds the result without ever calling sort.

This is [merge-intervals](merge-intervals)'s incremental sibling: same overlap logic, but applied to one insertion instead of a batch, and that difference is exactly what an interviewer is probing when they ask "what if intervals arrive one at a time?"

Because the existing list is sorted and already merged, every interval in it falls into exactly one of three zones relative to the new interval:

1. **Fully before** — its end is strictly less than the new interval's start. Copy it to the result unchanged.
2. **Overlapping** — its start is `<=` the new interval's (possibly already-extended) end, and its end is `>=` the new interval's start. Absorb it by growing the new interval's bounds.
3. **Fully after** — its start is strictly greater than the new interval's (final) end. Copy it unchanged.

The scan walks these zones in order — because the list is sorted, once you leave zone 1 you're in zone 2, and once you leave zone 2 you're in zone 3, never back. That single-direction guarantee is what keeps this O(n) with no sort needed.

slides.sectionTitle: The new interval growing as it absorbs
slides.markdown:
Picture the sorted list as a row of non-overlapping bars, and the new interval dropped in somewhere in the middle. As the scan reaches each bar that overlaps it, the new interval's own start shrinks to the min and its end grows to the max — it visibly widens to swallow each overlapping neighbor before moving on.

By the time the scan reaches a bar fully to the right, the new interval has finished growing and is inserted as one single merged block, with everything before and after copied through untouched.

![A new interval widening below the row to absorb the two intervals it overlaps, then replacing them in the final merged row](assets/insert-interval-absorb.svg)

slides.markdown:
```python
def insert(intervals, new_interval):
    result = []
    i, n = 0, len(intervals)
    new_start, new_end = new_interval

    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < new_start:
        result.append(intervals[i])           # zone 1: fully before
        i += 1

    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= new_end:
        new_start = min(new_start, intervals[i][0])
        new_end = max(new_end, intervals[i][1])
        i += 1                                  # zone 2: overlapping, absorb
    result.append([new_start, new_end])

    while i < n:
        result.append(intervals[i])            # zone 3: fully after
        i += 1

    return result
```

Three simple `while` loops, one index, no sort call — the shape mirrors the three zones exactly.

The easy-but-wasteful solution: append the new interval to the list and re-run [merge-intervals](merge-intervals) on the whole thing. It's correct — but it throws away the one fact that makes this problem different from Merge Intervals: **the existing list was already sorted and merged.**

Re-sorting a list that's already sorted costs O(n log n) for zero benefit, when a single O(n) pass would do. In an interview, proposing the append-and-remerge approach first is fine as a warm-up, but stopping there reads as not having noticed the given precondition. Naming the sorted precondition and the O(n) consequence is the actual signal the question is testing for.

A common off-by-logic bug: the code correctly copies the "before" zone, correctly absorbs the "overlapping" zone, appends the merged new interval — and then **stops**, forgetting that everything from the current index to the end of the list still needs to be copied through.

This silently drops the entire tail of the calendar whenever the new interval doesn't touch the last few entries. It's an easy miss because it only shows up when the new interval is inserted somewhere in the middle or near the front — test cases where the new interval overlaps the *last* existing interval hide the bug completely, since there's no tail left to forget.

Always include an explicit third loop (or equivalent) that flushes whatever remains after the merge window closes.

"Append then run Merge Intervals" is O(n log n) because it re-sorts data that didn't need sorting. Insert Interval's single pass is O(n) because it exploits the given order instead of discarding it.

The gap matters at scale: for a calendar with 10,000 already-merged events receiving a steady stream of single inserts, re-sorting each time costs roughly n log n ≈ 10,000 × 13 ≈ 130,000 comparison-scale operations per insert, versus roughly 10,000 for the single pass — over 10x more work, repeated on every single insertion. This is the general lesson of exploiting a precondition: when the problem hands you "already sorted" for free, spending an algorithm's complexity budget on re-establishing it is pure waste.

The pass above is O(n) time and O(n) space for the new result list, since it builds a fresh array rather than mutating in place. True in-place insertion is possible on some array representations (shift the tail to make room, similar to array insertion in general), but it costs O(n) *per insert* for the shift regardless — no asymptotic win, just less allocation churn.

If inserts are frequent and the calendar is large, this is the point where a production system would reach for a different data structure entirely — an interval tree or a balanced BST keyed by start — trading array simplicity for O(log n) insert and query. That trade-off, and when it's worth making, is exactly the kind of follow-up a senior interview pushes into.

[merge-intervals](merge-intervals) closed by noting that merging is fundamentally a batch operation. Insert Interval is the answer to "what do you do incrementally instead": maintain the invariant that the list is always merged, and fold each new arrival in with one O(n) pass rather than re-deriving the invariant from scratch every time.

This pattern — maintain a sorted invariant, fold in one new element at a time — generalizes well beyond intervals: it's the same idea behind inserting into a sorted array, a balanced tree, or a running median structure. Interviewers who ask "can you do this online?" are usually testing whether you reach for this shape by instinct.
